heading: Do noise and variance explain multiple peaks removed by optimally tuned overfitting controls?
definition: the peak is driven by label noise or variance, can split into several peaks (triple or multiple descent), and disappears under optimally tuned regularization.
summary: Independent studies support noise or variance mechanisms, multiple peaks, and removal by tuned regularization in specific settings. The general claim is contested: bias can diverge without label noise, and peaks can survive optimized input-noise regularization, although optimal ridge removes them in specified linear and random-feature settings.

suggested_status.by_scale: C for the unrestricted mechanism/removal statement in analytical and small-model settings, mostly with size unstated; ? for the complete conjunction at explicitly identified <1B scale. No identified V6 size coverage at 1-10B, 10-100B or >100B.
suggested_status.reason: The broad statement is contested by a noiseless bias divergence (arXiv:1908.05355#r2 and arXiv:1908.05355#r5) and persistence under optimized input-noise regularization (arXiv:2305.17297#R6). Specified optimal-ridge monotonicity remains supported (arXiv:2003.01897#r1, arXiv:2003.01897#r4 and arXiv:2003.01897#r7). The prediction-error upper bound under prescribed tuning in arXiv:2106.04795#r3 establishes neither an actual-risk peak nor its persistence under actual-risk-optimal regularization; it provides no directional verdict on that component of V6. counts: versions.V6.verdicts records support alongside challenges and scope limits; versions.V6.studies_by_size and versions.V6.coverage_by_operation.scaling.by_size identify only '<1B' and 'not stated'. This status applies to the unrestricted composite wording, not to rejection of its condition-specific dependencies.
suggested_status.open_questions: A same-setting end-to-end deep-network study controlling noise and variance sources, measuring multiple total-risk peaks, and optimizing a named regularizer against independently evaluated risk would clarify the combined claim. Matching decomposition conventions could clarify the bias/variance disagreement. Explicit model-size and training-stage coverage is needed beyond the identified small-model metadata.

source.title: Deep double descent: where bigger models and more data hurt
source.authors: Preetum Nakkiran; Gal Kaplun; Yamini Bansal; Tristan Yang; B. Barak; I. Sutskever

original_result.setup: The original study varied ResNet18 width on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
original_result.result: On CIFAR-10, test error peaked near interpolation with 15% label noise; without label noise and with augmentation, it plateaued. On CIFAR-100, a peak remained without label noise.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

wording_issues.phrase: driven by label noise or variance
wording_issues.issue: An exclusive mechanism statement does not fit the noiseless linear-target bias divergence, covariance-heterogeneity bias peaks or signal–covariance misalignment. The bias divergence is observed while the proposed noise-or-variance mechanism is contradicted under that decomposition. Noise-independent bias-component peaks support multiple descent at the component level; they do not establish a full risk curve across interpolation. Attribution requires the model assumptions and averaging convention.

Added corruption, intrinsic dataset errors, unlearned target modes, deterministic misspecification and initialization/sample variability are different conditions. Zero added corruption does not establish a noiseless target. Deterministic residuals can contribute variance, supporting V6's variance alternative rather than limiting it. High training-label noise largely suppresses stochastic-Adam best-loss double descent in DeepONet; this qualifies noise dependence without refuting V6, which does not predict monotonic strengthening with added noise.

The evidence generally establishes multiple peaks at distinct thresholds, not continuous splitting of one original peak as noise increases. Causes include separated feature scales, covariance subspaces, ℓ1 geometry and sparsity, staged learning, and distinct classical/quantum thresholds. Component-only peaks and selected examples need separate qualification.

Actual-risk minimization, test-error optimization, cross-validation, GCV, finite searches and rate-optimal tuning of an upper bound are different procedures. Finite-grid empirical ridge selection reports mitigation without establishing strict elimination or persistence. The rate-optimal ReLU upper bound establishes neither an actual-risk peak nor persistence under actual-risk-optimal tuning. ResNet-18 peaks persist under tested regularization settings, whose exact ablation grid is not reliably legible; disappearance under optimal tuning remains undetermined.

The optimized family and training stage must be named. Optimized input noise can leave a peak; joint ridge/input-noise grid search can remove it. That joint search uses μ in (0,100] and σ_trn/√n in (0,10], excluding zero from both ranges. Optimal target regularization can retain inherited source divergence, and teacher-only regularization can strengthen a student peak. These qualify a universal disappearance statement without refuting the specified optimal-ridge results.

Removing a singularity, attenuating a bump, removing the second descent and making risk monotone are distinct outcomes; V6 does not itself require monotonic risk. Intermediate regularization removes the second descent while conventional overfitting remains, supporting regularization dependence. Stronger fixed regularization can introduce final ascent. Positive ridge can leave finite quantum-regression peaks. These fixed-setting results do not test disappearance under optimally tuned regularization. Peak-free diffusion test loss can coexist with double descent in FID, so the outcome metric must be named.

The records mix total test/prediction error, variance or bias components, risk bounds and boundary mean dimension (BMD). Multiple component peaks support component-level multiple descent without establishing multiple total-risk peaks. The anisotropic-regression component sweeps examine only γ>1, leaving the full curve across interpolation undetermined. A variance upper bound alone does not establish an actual variance-driven risk peak. In the twin-peaks study, increasing λ suppresses the generalization-error peak at P=N; the secondary N=D peak belongs to BMD and is absent from generalization error. In BMD, the P=N peak disappears first.

method_sensitivity.factor: Noise level, noise type, width and sweep axis
method_sensitivity.what: ResNet18 epoch-wise noise onset depends on width: narrow models show little or no double descent across the tested fractions, while wider models develop peaks. In FCNN/CNN width sweeps, noise can create, amplify and move the peak. Adversarial and Gaussian input perturbations have different outcomes. Dense versus sparse pairwise Siamese label noise changes peak location and overparameterized error; dense noise retains a peak typically shifted toward larger widths, although training error does not vanish as width increases. Clean Siamese MLP/CNN width sweeps on MNIST, FMNIST and CIFAR10 also show peaks; a variance mechanism is not tested or excluded.

method_sensitivity.factor: Training versus evaluation label corruption and clean transfer targets
method_sensitivity.what: In binary CIFAR-10 validation-loss experiments, noisy training labels give a plateau with clean validation labels and double descent with noisy validation labels. Clean training labels give no double descent regardless of validation corruption. Separately, DenseNet-121 and ViT transfer experiments exhibit epoch-wise double descent on some noiseless target datasets. Those clean-target observations establish that added label noise is unnecessary in those settings; variance causation and optimally tuned regularization are not tested.

method_sensitivity.factor: Spectral gaps, covariance rank, component scales and mixture proportions
method_sensitivity.what: Small kernel gaps remove visible multiple descent. Separated random-feature scales alter peak count and prominence. In arXiv:2607.24041, the tested full-rank controls retain only the classical peak; near-degenerate directions can restore extra peaks. R24 has one peak at p/n=1, and R31 also lacks splitting, with angle endpoint approximately π/6; optimal regularization is untested. These covariance restrictions do not generalize to arXiv:2610.38002: its noiseless mixtures assume positive-definite covariances and show extra peaks with power-law spectra or positive isotropic covariance scales. At n=1000, changing group proportion p1 from 1/4 to 1/2 to 3/4 moves the extra peak from m=250 to 500 to 750; the classical peak remains at m=1000.

Finite averaging reduces RF peaks; infinite ensembling or bagging removes the identified divergent interaction terms. The RF decomposition identifies variance-driven noiseless divergence, exacerbated by label noise. At fixed label corruption, SWAG reduces ResNet-18/CIFAR-100 peaks and MultiSWAG removes them, supporting variance dependence. Self-adaptive target correction removes the width peak and largely removes the epoch-wise peak. Knowledge-distilled pruned students also avoid sparse double descent; these distillation results do not establish risk-optimal tuning. In ResNet-18/CIFAR-100 pruning with 50% label noise, sparse double descent persists under AutoAugment/CutOut, dropout 0.5, L1 at 10^-5 and L2 at 10^-4; L2 at 10^-3 shifts it left. These tested settings do not establish optimal tuning.

method_sensitivity.factor: Penalty-selection objective and tuning to noise/capacity
method_sensitivity.what: A per-width RF risk optimum gives a monotone envelope. Finite-grid empirical ridge selection mitigates MSE nonmonotonicity without establishing elimination or persistence. ViT pruning needs stronger tested regularization at 50% noise than at lower noise; peak removal supports regularization dependence. On ViT/CIFAR-10 with 10% label noise, default λ=0.03 full pruning yields 74.47±0.01% accuracy at 99.26% sparsity; λopt yields 71.48±0.06% at 86.58% sparsity. These selected settings incur performance/compressibility costs and do not establish a common pointwise risk-optimal protocol. DeiT-Tiny LoRA finite validation selection reduces the rank-dependent rise from 0.53 to 0.16 nats, with every selected checkpoint below 99% training accuracy. Tested weight-decay coefficients preserve its cliff. These DeiT experiments do not establish disappearance or failure of disappearance under actual-risk-optimal tuning.

method_sensitivity.factor: Which regularizer and which training stage are optimized
method_sensitivity.what: Joint ridge/input-noise optimization differs from input-noise-only optimization: the joint grid uses μ in (0,100] and σ_trn/√n in (0,10], excluding zero. Target-transfer regularization can leave inherited source error; teacher regularization differs from direct student regularization. For batch methods, optimizing asymptotic risk upper bounds yields SNR-dependent behavior: optimized BMN remains nonmonotonic below ξ≈0.6478, while optimized SBMN removes the peak. Fixed-b=2 Wiener-shrinkage and batch experiments show post-interpolation improvement followed by an eventual rise; they do not test peak removal under optimal batch-size tuning.

Diffusion test-loss stopping removes the test-loss peak while FID retains double descent. Best-epoch selection removes reported size nonmonotonicity in Tiny Shakespeare models. Fourier-feature risk rescaling prevents comparison of noise effects on peak height and leaves the V6 mechanism undetermined. In the RFM sample-count sweep, N and D are fixed with D/N=0.1, MSE, tanh activation and λ=10^-4: a secondary test-loss peak at P=D is absent at Δ=0 and present at Δ=5. Separately, increasing λ suppresses the generalization-error peak at P=N. The secondary N=D peak belongs to BMD and is absent from generalization error; within BMD, the P=N peak disappears before the N=D peak.

method_sensitivity.factor: Loss, feature learning, preprocessing and initialization
method_sensitivity.what: Noiseless square-loss RF classification retains a peak while its logistic-loss counterpart lacks one; these fixed-regularization comparisons do not test optimal peak removal or exclude variance. Task-optimized nonlinearities remove synthetic classification peaks; real-image experiments with normalizing-flow preprocessing report mitigation without establishing whether a peak remains. Learned Bayesian linear networks lack the noiseless sample-wise divergence of fixed-feature bottlenecks, whose divergence is attributed to feature–data randomness interactions. NTK peak structure varies with SNR, centering and second-layer initialization variance. With tanh activation, decreasing second-layer initialization variance increases the quadratic-transition hump as the kernel approaches K2; ridge strength is unstated for that panel.

In weakly correlated QELMs, fewer shots lower the interpolation peak across the stated m0=10², 10³ and 10⁴ comparison; a noiseless empirical-risk baseline is unspecified. In strongly correlated QELMs, finite-shot features suppress an additional peak while retaining the interpolation peak. In quantum linear regression, finite training shots instead create a distinct quantum peak absent with exact features. Positive ridge rounds interpolation poles into finite peaks. At fixed nout=ntr=1024, ridge first decreases then increases MSE, and the minimizing displayed ridge depends on test-shot budget M. This fixed-setting optimization does not determine peak elimination across model complexity under optimal regularization.

method_sensitivity.factor: Basis construction, spectral cutoff and reconstruction priors
method_sensitivity.what: In arXiv:2304.08113 Case A, linear basis ordering gives a noisy NMSE peak at n=N=10; optimal ordering substantially reduces variance and inverse-smallest-singular-value amplification, with noisy NMSE comparable to noise-free NMSE, but complete peak removal is undetermined. Cutting small singular values removes regression peaks in arXiv:2303.14151. In arXiv:2307.11838 SST sensor-count sweeps, isotropic placement plus isotropic reconstruction slightly suppresses the peak; the other prior combinations are monotonic. POD placement with isotropic reconstruction is Fig. S2d, and POD placement with POD reconstruction is Fig. S2b. Separately, arXiv:2607.26414 uses POD-informed anisotropic regularization: under-regularization produces peaks, whereas optimal and over-regularization yield monotonic curves. Its random placement produces an early spike at p=24; removing both noise and residual-mode contamination gives exact reconstruction for p≥r.

method_sensitivity.factor: Tested penalties, pruning persistence and conventional overfitting
method_sensitivity.what: ResNet-18/CIFAR-10/100 pruning double descent persists at tested ℓ2 λ=10^-4 and under the reported λ ablation; the exact ablation grid is not reliably legible. ResNet34/CIFAR-10 width sweeps with MSE and 20% symmetric label noise show double descent at λ=0.0005 and final ascent at λ=0.001. In ResNet18/CIFAR-10 with 15% label noise and a linear teacher–student model with κ=100, intermediate regularization removes epoch-wise second descent while retaining decrease-then-increase overfitting. In synthetic DeepSurv with Gaussian covariates and 30% censoring, weight decay 0.01 leaves the C-index minimum at width 16; reported attenuation is nonsignificant at p=0.06. None establishes disappearance or persistence under optimal tuning.

method_sensitivity.factor: Threshold-dependent attenuation, spectral decay and task coupling
method_sensitivity.what: In RF and three-layer teacher–student networks at SNR=0.2, finite ensembling with K=10 and fixed penalties attenuate the nonlinear triple-descent peak much more than the linear peak. RF ridge γ increases from 10^-5 to 10^-3; the network weight-decay comparison uses γ=0.05. In KRR, moderate regularization shifts the variance peak toward smaller sample sizes; exponential eigenvalue decay removes the variance-bound peak even at tiny regularization, a result distinct from total risk. In squared-loss multi-task regression with T=3 and γ1 fixed at 10^-2, varying coupling γ2 moves the peak and changes its height nonmonotonically without removing it. These finite or fixed-parameter comparisons do not test optimal peak elimination.

In two-layer ReLU square-loss theory with class probability ρ₁=0.7 and α=n/d, λ≥1 produces an initial plateau followed by declining error. Stronger regularization delays improvement; at λ=100, decline begins around α≈60. This cost concerns excessive regularization and does not establish a limitation of optimal tuning.
